opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing. I'm not sure human mathematical skills, in the narrow sense of producing proofs, remain *economically* valuable in the long run if models become genuinely superhuman across the board. If an AI system can do what a strong research mathematician does, faster and cheaper, the market value of that specific labor is going to fall, just like it has for many other tasks that got automated.

But there are a few reasons I still think the skills matter, at least for a while and in certain ways.

First, there's a gap between being superhuman at math benchmarks and being superhuman at *doing mathematics* in the full sense. Solving well-posed competition problems is one thing. Deciding which questions are worth asking, which definitions are the right ones, and how a result fits into a broader research program is a different capability. Models may get there too, but I expect that part to lag, and humans who understand the field deeply will be the ones directing and evaluating the work in the meantime.

Second, verification and judgment. If a model hands you a hundred-page argument, someone has to decide whether to trust it, how to formalize it, or what it actually implies. Proof assistants help a lot, but you still need people who understand what's being claimed, especially when the math feeds into decisions in physics, engineering, cryptography, or AI safety itself.

Third, mathematical training is really a way of learning to think clearly: to reason carefully about assumptions, spot when an argument doesn't follow, and build quantitative models of the world. That's useful well beyond proving theorems. A lot of my own work involves forecasting and economic modeling of AI, and the habits I picked up from math are central to it, even though I'm not proving anything.

And finally, there's intrinsic value. People still play chess even though engines have been far better for decades. Understanding a beautiful proof is a human experience, and that doesn't disappear because a machine found it first.

So my honest view is that the comparative advantage of humans will shift from generating mathematics toward steering, interpreting, and appreciating it, and eventually even some of that may be automated. But the underlying skill of rigorous thinking will stay valuable for a good while.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human judgment and mathematical training, but does not say a person's own math ability is easier to integrate into their workflow than an AI model's ability.

r002.rationale: It says people who understand the field deeply will direct and evaluate model work, and describes choosing worthwhile questions and definitions as part of that direction.

r003.rationale: The response says someone must decide whether to trust a model's argument, but does not state that lacking mathematical knowledge makes its mistakes difficult to detect.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm not actually sure they will remain valuable in every sense. If you mean economically valuable, as in people being paid to prove theorems, I think that could go away fairly quickly once models are genuinely better at it than humans. So I want to separate that from a few other senses in which the skills still matter.

One is that mathematical skill isn't really about producing proofs. It's about being able to recognize when a claim is true, when an argument is sound, and what question is even worth asking. Even if a model can do the deductive work much faster than you, you still have to decide what you want from it and whether the answer it gives you is the thing you actually asked for. People who can't do that at all are in a bad position, because they're totally dependent on the system's framing. You see this already with people using models for coding. The ones who can read the code and spot when something is subtly wrong get a lot more out of the tools than the ones who can't.

The second thing is that mathematics is one of the main ways we have of thinking clearly about anything. If you want to reason about economics, or about AI itself, or about how the world might go over the next few decades, you need some comfort with quantitative reasoning, with abstraction, with knowing what follows from what. That's a general cognitive skill, and the fact that a machine can also do it doesn't make it useless for you, in the same way that calculators didn't make arithmetic intuition useless. It made it less of a bottleneck, but people who have no feel for numbers still make bad decisions.

And then there's a third point, which is more about what we value. Chess is the standard example here. Engines have been better than every human for decades and the game is more popular than ever, because people care about humans doing it. I'm not saying math will go exactly the same way, but I'd be surprised if the activity of understanding something for yourself just stopped being meaningful to people because a model got there first.

So my view is roughly: the marginal product of a human mathematician in the sense of generating new results probably declines a lot. But the skill of thinking mathematically stays valuable because it's what lets you use these systems well, and because understanding things is something people want for its own sake. Whether that shows up in wages is a separate question, and I'm fairly skeptical that it will.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical skill helps people use models, but does not state that a person’s own ability is easier to integrate into their normal workflow than math supplied by a model.

r002.rationale: It says mathematical skill helps people decide what they want from a model and assess whether its answer is what they asked for.

r003.rationale: It says mathematical skill lets people recognize whether claims are true and arguments sound, while people who cannot do that are dependent on the system’s framing. In context, this conveys difficulty spotting a model’s mathematical errors.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between being able to solve a mathematical problem and being able to judge which problems are worth solving. Even if a model is much better than you at finding proofs, you still benefit from understanding enough mathematics to ask useful questions and interpret the answers.

Suppose you're trying to understand some economic phenomenon. A model might solve whatever formal problem you give it, but did you choose assumptions that capture the thing you actually care about? What does the result tell you about the world? Mathematical understanding helps you move between those questions and the formal machinery.

And superhuman doesn't mean infallible. You don't necessarily need to check every step yourself, but having some independent understanding helps you notice when an answer is surprising or when you should ask for a different explanation.

Of course, if models become better at choosing problems and interpreting results as well, the case for human mathematical skill as an economically useful input becomes weaker. I wouldn't claim otherwise. But understanding something can still be valuable to you even when there's another entity that understands it better. We don't learn mathematics solely to be the best mathematician in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical understanding helps people ask useful questions and interpret answers, but it does not say a person's own ability is easier to integrate into their normal workflow than a model's ability.

r002.rationale: It says understanding mathematics helps people ask useful questions and choose assumptions that capture what they care about, which communicates that expertise helps direct a model toward desired results.

r003.rationale: It says independent understanding can help someone notice surprising answers, but does not clearly state that lacking mathematical knowledge makes it difficult to detect the model's mathematical mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think being able to solve a mathematical problem and being able to decide which mathematical problems are worth solving are different things. Even if a model is much better than you at the first, you still need some understanding to connect its work to something you actually care about.

Suppose you’re trying to understand an economic question. You can ask the model to analyze a particular setup, and it might do that perfectly. But are the assumptions sensible? Does the result tell you what you wanted to know? Often the difficulty is in that translation between the real world and the formal problem. Mathematical understanding helps you make that translation and ask useful follow-up questions.

Now, you could imagine models becoming better at all of those things as well. I don’t think there’s some permanent boundary where humans necessarily retain an advantage. But even then, mathematical skill can help you understand the answers you’re getting and make informed decisions about them. The fact that someone else can do something better doesn’t make your own understanding worthless.

r001.rationale: The response says personal understanding helps connect a model’s work to what one cares about, but does not compare workflow integration with model-supplied ability.

r002.rationale: It says understanding helps assess assumptions, judge whether results answer the intended question, and ask useful follow-up questions, describing how mathematical expertise can direct the model toward desired results.

r003.rationale: The response mentions understanding and evaluating answers, but does not say mathematical knowledge helps detect mathematical mistakes in the model’s work.
